blocks.text: Make a thread wait until a condition on shared state holds before it proceeds.

A **guarded method** checks a **precondition** under a lock. While it is false, the thread **suspends** and releases the lock. Another thread changes the state and **signals**; the waiter wakes, reacquires the lock, and checks the guard again. State and guard live together in one monitor.

items: **Guard:** a boolean condition over state protected by the lock.
**Wait in a loop:** `while`, never `if`; wakeups can be spurious or stolen.
**Signal on every change** that can make some guard true.

blocks.text: `wait` releases the monitor and reacquires it before returning. Writes made before `notifyAll` by the signaler are visible to the waiter afterwards.

walkthrough.note: The guard `item == null` is rechecked in a `while` loop after every wakeup. `wait()` releases the monitor, so a producer can enter `put`.
The producer has its own guard: the slot must be empty. Changing `item` and then calling `notifyAll()` wakes threads whose guard may now hold.
The consumer starts first and blocks on the empty slot. Restoring the interrupt flag keeps cancellation visible to callers.
The main thread produces. Whatever order the scheduler picks, each guard is evaluated under the lock, so the result is the same.
`join` gives a happens-before edge, so reading `received` here is safe. The list needed no extra synchronization.

blocks.text: Borrowing a connection from a database pool.

A request thread calls `borrow()` when all connections are in use. It must block until one is returned, but not forever: after 30 seconds the call fails so the request can return an error instead of hanging. The guard is `!idle.isEmpty()`, `return()` signals, and the wait is a timed `awaitNanos` that survives spurious wakeups by recomputing the remaining time.
Payoff: waiters sleep without burning CPU, and the bounded wait turns pool exhaustion into a fast, handled failure.

lists.title: Use when
items: A thread cannot proceed until another thread changes shared state.
The wait should consume no CPU, unlike polling.
Several conditions share one lock and need separate wait sets.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: A `BlockingQueue`, `CountDownLatch` or `Future` already expresses the wait.
The caller can proceed without the result: use a callback or a non-blocking check.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Using `if` instead of `while`: spurious or stolen wakeups break the guard.
Forgetting to signal after a state change, which leaves waiters stuck forever.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: One lock with many unrelated guards and `notifyAll` storming every waiter.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: `ReentrantLock` with `Condition` gives several wait sets and timed waits.
Blocking inside `synchronized` pins a virtual thread in Java 21; prefer `ReentrantLock` conditions or `java.util.concurrent` types there.

rows.difference: A blocking queue is guarded suspension on both ends: `take` waits while empty, `put` waits while full.
A future packages one result and lets the caller wait for it, or compose without waiting. Guarded suspension waits on arbitrary shared state, repeatedly.
A guard should be bounded. A timed wait with remaining-time bookkeeping stops a missed signal becoming a hung thread.
An active object takes the request on its own thread, so the caller need not block on a condition at all.

entries.name: Object.wait / notifyAll
entries.detail: The primitive form: `wait` releases the monitor, and the javadoc requires calling it in a loop.

entries.name: java.util.concurrent.locks.Condition
entries.detail: `await`, `awaitNanos` and `signalAll` provide multiple wait sets per `ReentrantLock`.

entries.name: ArrayBlockingQueue
entries.detail: `take` and `put` wait on `Condition` objects (`notEmpty`, `notFull`) guarded by one lock.

entries.name: CountDownLatch
entries.detail: `await` blocks until the count reaches zero, a one-shot guard.

options.why: Threads block while a condition on shared state is false and are woken when another thread changes it.
It looks like a repeated check, but this waits for a signal; DCL avoids locking for one-time initialization.
There is no queue of work items moving between threads, only a single flag.
All access takes the same exclusive monitor; there is no shared read mode.

exercises.scenario: A worker thread must not start sending until a separate thread finishes the handshake. The handshake flag is shared state; the worker should sleep, not poll, and may be reused for many handshakes.

options.why: The worker waits on a condition over shared state and is signaled when the handshake changes it.
A pool reuses threads for tasks; it does not make one thread wait for a condition.
Immutable data needs no waiting, but here the point is waiting for a change.
It governs concurrent access modes and has no way to wait until a condition becomes true.

exercises.prompt: Tap the line that breaks Guarded Suspension.
exercises.explanation: The guard is checked once. After a spurious wakeup, or if another consumer took the item first, the thread proceeds with `null`. Use `while (item == null) wait();`.

exercises.prompt: Order the body of the guarded take so that the state stays consistent.
exercises.explanation: Wait for the guard first, read the item, then clear it. Signal after the state change so woken threads see it, and return last.

exercises.prompt: Explain Guarded Suspension in your own words: why a loop, and what wait does with the lock.

modelAnswer.text: A thread tests a condition on shared state under a lock and, if false, waits, which releases the lock. Another thread changes the state and signals. The waiter reacquires the lock and rechecks in a loop, because wakeups can be spurious or the condition may already be consumed.

keyPoints: Guard and state protected by the same lock
wait releases the lock and reacquires it before returning
Always recheck the guard in a while loop
Signal after every state change that can satisfy a guard
Bound the wait and handle interruption
